roleplay.title: Chest pressure with walking
roleplay.setup: You are the cardiologist. A man was referred for chest pain. Take the full story: onset, character, location and radiation, duration, triggers and relief, and associated symptoms.
roleplay.persona: You play Don Arturo Salinas, 62, from Michoacán, Mexico; you work in construction in Chicago. For about three weeks ('desde hace como tres semanas') you get a pressure in the middle of the chest, 'como un peso', when you walk uphill, climb stairs, or carry heavy material at work. It sometimes goes to your left arm. It lasts about five minutes and goes away when you stop and rest. Sometimes you sweat with it. The last time was yesterday at work while carrying cement bags (keep it simple: 'estaba en el trabajo'). Severity about 6 out of 10. You have no pain now and never had pain at rest. No fainting. Speak in simple sentences using the preterite for events (empezó, me dio, duró, se me quitó) and short imperfect chunks for background (estaba). Only reveal the arm radiation, the sweating and the severity number if asked. If asked something you don't understand, say '¿Mande?'.
roleplay.opening: Buenos días, doctor. Mi doctor me mandó aquí por un dolor en el pecho.
goals: Find out when the pain first started and when the last episode was
Ask what the pain feels like and whether it spreads anywhere
Ask what brings it on and what makes it go away
Ask how long an episode lasts and how strong it is from 0 to 10
Ask about associated symptoms such as sweating, nausea or shortness of breath

roleplay.title: Episodes of a racing heart
roleplay.setup: A woman reports episodes of a fast heartbeat. Find out when they began, how they start and stop, how long they last, what she was doing during the last one, and what came with it.
roleplay.persona: You play Guadalupe Reyes, 45, from Tegucigalpa, Honduras; you work as a cook. The episodes started about six months ago ('hace como seis meses'). The heart suddenly races, fast and regular, 'como si me fuera a salir del pecho' — but say simply 'el corazón me late muy rápido'. Each episode starts suddenly and stops suddenly, lasting about 20 minutes. Sometimes it stops if you cough hard. The last episode was three days ago, in the evening, while you were sitting watching TV ('estaba sentada en la sala'). During episodes you feel a little dizzy and anxious but you have never fainted and have no chest pain. No episodes right now. Use the preterite for events and only short imperfect chunks (estaba) for background. Reveal the coughing trick and the dizziness only if the doctor asks what makes it stop or what other symptoms you had.
roleplay.opening: Buenas tardes, doctor. A veces el corazón me late muy rápido y me asusto.
goals: Find out how long ago the episodes started and when the last one was
Ask whether they start and stop suddenly or gradually, and how long they last
Ask what she was doing when the last episode started
Ask what makes an episode stop

title: Cardiac review of symptoms
goal: Run a full cardiac review of symptoms: chest pain, breathlessness, swelling, palpitations, dizziness and fainting, and how far the patient can walk.

grammar.p: Many symptoms use the *gustar* pattern: the symptom is the subject and the person is *me / le*. *Me falta el aire* is literally 'air is lacking to me'. The verb agrees with the symptom: *me duele la pierna* but *me duelen las piernas*. For swelling, patients say *se me hinchan los pies* (my feet swell); you ask *¿Se le hinchan los pies?*
ex: ¿Le falta el aire cuando camina?
Are you short of breath when you walk?
¿Se le hinchan los tobillos en la tarde?
Do your ankles swell in the afternoon?
Me duelen las pantorrillas cuando camino.
My calves hurt when I walk.

grammar.h: Triggers: al + infinitive, cuando, en reposo
grammar.p: To ask what brings a symptom on, use *al* + infinitive (*al caminar* = when walking) or *cuando* + present (*cuando sube escaleras*). Contrast *con el esfuerzo* (with exertion) and *en reposo* (at rest). *Hasta* means 'even': *hasta en reposo* = even at rest.
ex: ¿Le falta el aire al subir escaleras?
Do you get short of breath climbing stairs?
¿Le da dolor de pecho con el esfuerzo?
Do you get chest pain with exertion?
Me falta el aire hasta en reposo.
I'm short of breath even at rest.

grammar.h: The fainting story: imperfect for the scene, preterite for the event
grammar.p: Use the imperfect for the background (where the patient was, what they were doing, what it was like): *estaba, hacía, había*. Use the preterite for what happened: *me mareé, me desmayé, me caí, me golpeé*. A closed period with a measured length also takes the preterite: *¿Cuánto tiempo estuvo inconsciente?*
ex: ¿Qué hacía cuando se desmayó?
What were you doing when you fainted?
Estaba en la iglesia y hacía mucho calor.
I was in church and it was very hot.
Me mareé, se me nubló la vista y me caí.
I got dizzy, my vision went dim, and I fell.

grammar.p: Measure function with *cuadras* (blocks), *pisos* (floors) and *escaleras* (stairs). Compare with the past using the imperfect for 'used to': *Antes caminaba diez cuadras; ahora camino dos.* *Podía* = 'I used to be able to'.
ex: ¿Cuántas cuadras puede caminar sin parar?
How many blocks can you walk without stopping?
Antes subía tres pisos sin problema.
I used to climb three floors without a problem.
Ahora me canso más que antes.
Now I get tired more than before.

grammar.p: Patients describe the heartbeat as *rápido* (fast), *acelerado* (racing), *fuerte* (pounding), *irregular*, or as *brincos* (skips, jumps). Here *lo* means 'it' (the heart): *¿Lo siente rápido?* = Do you feel it fast?
ex: ¿Siente el corazón rápido, fuerte o irregular?
Do you feel your heart fast, pounding, or irregular?
Siento brincos en el pecho.
I feel skips in my chest.
El corazón me late muy rápido.
My heart beats very fast.

roleplay.title: Breathless and swollen
roleplay.setup: You are the cardiologist seeing a new patient referred for shortness of breath. Find out when he gets short of breath, how he sleeps, whether he has swelling, and how far he can walk now compared with before.
roleplay.persona: You are José Martínez, 68, originally from Michoacán, Mexico, living in Chicago for 30 years, retired from restaurant work. Over the last two or three months you have gotten short of breath more and more easily. Facts: you used to walk about ten blocks to church; now you stop after one block because of breathlessness (not pain). You now sleep with three pillows and sometimes in the armchair. Two or three nights a week you wake up suddenly short of breath and have to sit up. Your ankles and feet swell, worse in the afternoon; your shoes feel tight. You get tired easily. No chest pain, no fainting, no palpitations. Speak simple Mexican Spanish at an intermediate level: present, preterite and imperfect, short sentences, everyday words (cuadras, almohadas, me falta el aire, se me hinchan los pies). Use usted with the doctor. Answer only what is asked; reveal the night-time waking and the swelling only if the doctor asks about sleep at night or about the feet/legs. If the doctor uses tú, answer normally but sound slightly surprised.
roleplay.opening: Buenas tardes, doctor. Vengo porque me canso mucho y me falta el aire.
goals: Ask whether the breathlessness comes with exertion, at rest, or lying down
Find out how many pillows he uses to sleep
Ask whether he wakes up at night short of breath
Ask about swelling of the feet or ankles and when it is worse
Compare how many blocks he can walk now versus before

roleplay.title: A faint at church
roleplay.setup: You are the electrophysiologist seeing a woman who fainted three days ago. Get the full fainting history: the setting, warning signs, how long she was out, injuries, and what the witness saw.
roleplay.persona: You are Rosa Pérez, 55, from Guatemala, living in Chicago, works cleaning offices. Three days ago you fainted at a long Sunday Mass: the church was very hot and crowded and you had been standing for a long time. Before fainting you felt hot, sweaty, nauseated, and your vision went dim. You fell and hit your left elbow (bruised, not broken); you did not hit your head. Your daughter saw it and says you were out for a few seconds, you looked very pale, and you woke up quickly and knew where you were. You did not lose control of your bladder and did not bite your tongue. No palpitations or chest pain before. You fainted once before as a teenager, also standing in a hot place. Speak simple Spanish at an intermediate level: present, preterite and imperfect, short sentences. Use usted with the doctor. Answer only what is asked; do not volunteer the earlier faint or the elbow injury unless asked about past episodes or injuries.
roleplay.opening: Doctor, el domingo me desmayé en la iglesia y mi hija se asustó mucho.
goals: Find out what she was doing and where she was when she fainted
Ask what she felt before the faint (warning signs)
Ask how long she was unconscious and how she was when she woke up
Ask whether she hit her head or got hurt
Ask whether anyone saw it and whether it has happened before

title: Medicines and history
goal: Take a medication list and check adherence, screen for bleeding on blood thinners, tell allergies from side effects, and take past medical, family and social history.

grammar.p: Form: *he / ha / han* + participle (*-ado / -ido*). With patients use *ha*: *¿Ha tenido…?* Key irregular participles: *hecho* (hacer), *dicho* (decir), *visto* (ver), *puesto* (poner), *muerto* (morir). Use it with *alguna vez*, *nunca*, *últimamente*, *ya*, *todavía no*. In Mexico you will also hear the preterite in these questions (*¿Alguna vez tuvo un infarto?*); both are understood, but this level practices the present perfect.
ex: ¿Alguna vez ha tenido un infarto?
Have you ever had a heart attack?
¿Le han hecho alguna operación?
Have you had any surgery?
Nunca he fumado.
I've never smoked.

grammar.h: Se me olvida: forgetting without blame
grammar.p: *Se me olvida* is literally 'it slips my mind' — it sounds gentle, so it is the best way to ask about missed doses. It works like *gustar*: *se le olvida* + an infinitive or a singular noun, *se le olvidan* + a plural noun. Past: *se me olvidó* (once), *se me olvidaron* (several things).
ex: ¿Se le olvida tomar la pastilla?
Do you forget to take the pill?
A veces se me olvidan las pastillas de la noche.
Sometimes I forget my evening pills.
Ayer se me olvidó la pastilla de la mañana.
Yesterday I forgot my morning pill.

grammar.h: How long: desde hace, hace … que, llevar
grammar.p: For something still going on, Spanish uses the PRESENT: *Tomo la pastilla desde hace dos años* or *Hace dos años que tomo la pastilla* (I've been taking it for two years). *Llevar* + time + *con* is very natural for conditions: *Llevo diez años con diabetes.* But *hace* + time with the PRETERITE means 'ago': *Dejé de fumar hace cinco años.*
ex: ¿Desde cuándo tiene la presión alta?
How long have you had high blood pressure?
Llevo cinco años con diabetes.
I've had diabetes for five years.
Me operaron hace tres años.
I had surgery three years ago.

grammar.p: Patients often say *soy alérgico/alérgica* for any bad reaction, so always ask *¿Qué le pasó cuando la tomó?* Hives (*ronchas*), swelling of the face or lips (*se me hinchó la cara / los labios*) or trouble breathing suggest a true allergy. A cough, upset stomach, dizziness or muscle aches (*me dio tos, me dolía el estómago, me mareaba*) are usually side effects (*efectos secundarios*). *Me cayó mal* is vague — always ask what happened.
ex: ¿Qué le pasó cuando la tomó?
What happened when you took it?
Me salieron ronchas y se me hinchó la cara.
I broke out in hives and my face swelled.
La pastilla me da tos.
The pill gives me a cough.

grammar.p: *Tomar* means both 'to take' (medicine) and 'to drink' (alcohol): *¿Toma alcohol?* For medicine changes use *ir a* + infinitive (*Vamos a revisar sus medicinas*) and *acabar de* + infinitive for 'just' (*Acabo de empezar una pastilla nueva*). *Dejar de* + infinitive = to stop doing something (*dejé de fumar*).
ex: ¿Toma alcohol? ¿Cuántas cervezas a la semana?
Do you drink alcohol? How many beers a week?
Vamos a revisar sus medicinas una por una.
We're going to go over your medicines one by one.
Acabo de empezar una pastilla para el colesterol.
I just started a cholesterol pill.

items.q: ¿Se le ___ tomar las pastillas?
items.qen: Do you forget to take your pills?
items.why: The thing that 'slips your mind' is the action tomar (an infinitive), which counts as singular → se le olvida.

items.q: A veces se me ___ las pastillas de la noche.
items.qen: Sometimes I forget my evening pills.
items.why: Las pastillas (plural) is the subject → se me olvidan; a veces signals a habit → present.

items.q: How do you ask a patient 'Have you ever had a heart attack?'
opts: ¿Va a tener alguna vez un infarto?
items.why: 'Have you ever' → present perfect; usted → ha tenido (has = tú).

items.q: A patient says: «Con esa pastilla me salieron ronchas y se me hinchó la cara.» This is most likely:
opts: A side effect, not an allergy
A sign that the pill is not working

items.q: A patient says: «La pastilla para la presión me da una tos seca.» How do you classify this?
opts: A side effect of the pill
items.why: A dry cough from a blood pressure pill is a side effect (efecto secundario), not an allergy.

items.q: Tomo la pastilla ___ hace cinco años.
items.qen: I've been taking the pill for five years.
items.why: Present tense + desde hace + time = something still going on: 'for five years'.

items.q: Llevo diez años ___ diabetes.
items.qen: I've had diabetes for ten years.
items.why: Llevar + time + con + condition: Llevo diez años con diabetes.

items.q: How do you ask a patient 'Have you ever smoked?'
items.why: Usted → ha; the participle never changes after haber → fumado.

items.q: What does «¿Cuántas cervezas toma a la semana?» mean?

How many beers do you drink a day?

items.why: Tomar = to drink (alcohol); present tense; a la semana = per week.

items.q: How do you ask 'Have you noticed blood in your urine?'
items.why: Urine = la orina. Encías = gums, heces = stool.

items.q: A patient says: «Mi papá tuvo una embolia.» In everyday Mexican Spanish this usually means he had:
items.why: Patients commonly use embolia (or derrame cerebral) to mean a stroke. Heart attack = infarto.

items.q: Which question screens for sleep apnea?

¿Ronca mucho o deja de respirar cuando duerme?

items.q: How do you ask a patient 'Has anyone in your family died suddenly at a young age?'
opts: ¿Alguien en tu familia ha muerto joven y de repente?
¿Alguien en su familia ha morido joven y de repente?
¿Alguien en su familia va a morir de repente?
¿Alguien en su familia ha muerto joven y de repente?
items.why: Usted (su familia), present perfect with the irregular participle muerto (not morido).

items.q: Acabo de ___ una medicina nueva.
items.qen: I just started a new medicine.
items.why: Acabar de is always followed by an infinitive: acabo de empezar.

items.q: A patient says: «Tomo una pastilla para adelgazar la sangre.» What is she taking?
items.why: Adelgazar la sangre = thin the blood. (Adelgazar alone also means 'lose weight' — don't be fooled.)

items.q: ¿Ya ___ la pastilla de hoy?
items.qen: Have you taken today's pill yet?
items.why: Ya ('yet/already') with a completed action up to now → present perfect: ha tomado.

items.q: How do you ask a patient 'Have you had any surgery?'
items.why: Present perfect with the irregular participle hecho: ¿Le han hecho…? (Hacido does not exist.)

items.why: Usted, present tense → vive.

items.q: Which is the best non-judgmental way to ask about missed doses?
opts: A muchas personas se les olvida alguna pastilla. ¿A usted le pasa?
items.why: It normalizes forgetting and uses usted. The others accuse the patient or use tú.

items.qen: Are you allergic to penicillin? (to a woman)
items.why: Speaking to one woman → feminine singular: alérgica.

items.q: ¿Alguna vez le ___ un marcapasos?
items.en: Have you ever had a pacemaker put in? (lit. Have they ever put a pacemaker in you?)
items.why: Ellos form of the present perfect; poner → puesto (irregular).

items.q: Acabo ___ empezar una pastilla nueva.
items.en: I just started a new pill.
items.why: Acabar de + infinitive = to have just done something.

items.q: Mañana usted ___ a empezar la pastilla nueva.

items.why: Usted + ir a + infinitive → va a empezar.

items.why: Morir has an irregular participle: muerto.

items.q: Mi abuela tuvo un ___ cerebral.

roleplay.title: Medication review on a blood thinner
roleplay.setup: You are the electrophysiologist seeing a patient with atrial fibrillation who brought her pill bottles. Go through what each pill is for, how she takes it and how often she forgets, screen for bleeding, and sort out her 'allergies'.
roleplay.persona: You are Teresa Flores, 72, from Jalisco, Mexico, living in Chicago with your husband. You have atrial fibrillation, high blood pressure, diabetes and high cholesterol. You don't know the names of your medicines; you describe them by purpose: one 'para adelgazar la sangre' (twice a day), one 'para el corazón', one 'para la presión', one 'para el azúcar' and one 'para el colesterol'. You forget the evening blood thinner two or three times a week because you fall asleep watching TV. Your gums bleed a little when you brush and you get bruises on your arms easily; no nosebleeds, no blood in the urine, no black stools. You say you are 'alérgica' to two things: penicillin (as a child you broke out in hives and your face swelled — a true allergy) and an earlier cholesterol pill that made your legs ache (a side effect; your doctor changed it). You also take a cinnamon tea and vitamins from the health-food store, but you only mention them if asked about non-prescription products or teas. Never state doses in milligrams. Speak simple Mexican Spanish at an intermediate level: present, preterite, imperfect, present perfect and 'ir a'. Use usted with the doctor. Answer only what you are asked.
roleplay.opening: Buenos días, doctor. Aquí le traje todas mis pastillas, pero no me sé los nombres.
goals: Find out what each pill is for and how often she takes it
Ask in a non-judgmental way how often she forgets a dose, and why
Screen for bleeding: gums, nose, bruises, urine, black stools
Ask what happened with each 'allergy' and tell allergy from side effect
Ask about over-the-counter medicines, vitamins and teas

roleplay.title: Full history for palpitations
roleplay.setup: You are seeing a new patient referred for palpitations. Before the exam, take his past medical history, surgeries, family history and social history.
roleplay.persona: You are Luis Castillo, 48, from El Salvador, living in Chicago with your wife and two teenage children. You drive a delivery truck, often at night. Past history: high blood pressure for about five years (you take one pill, but you forget it on weekends) and high cholesterol (diet only). You snore loudly and your wife says you sometimes stop breathing at night; you feel sleepy while driving in the afternoon. You have never been told you have sleep apnea. You have never had a heart attack or stroke. Surgery: appendix removed as a child; no heart procedures. Family: your father died suddenly in his sleep at 45 — nobody knew why; your older brother has a pacemaker. Social: you smoke about half a pack a day for twenty years, drink six to eight beers on Saturdays, drink energy drinks at work, and do not use drugs. No regular exercise. No known drug allergies. Speak simple Central American Spanish at an intermediate level (present, preterite, imperfect, present perfect, ir a). Use usted with the doctor. Reveal the snoring and pauses only if asked about sleep or snoring; reveal your father's sudden death only if asked about family history; mention energy drinks only if asked about caffeine, drinks, or what you drink at work.
roleplay.opening: Buenas tardes, doctor. Mi doctor me mandó porque a veces siento el corazón muy rápido.
goals: Ask about high blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol, heart attack, stroke and thyroid
Screen for sleep apnea (snoring, pauses in breathing, daytime sleepiness)
Ask about past surgeries and heart procedures
Ask about sudden death or heart problems in the family
Take a social history: smoking, alcohol, drugs, work and who he lives with

title: Exam and tests
goal: Guide a patient through the physical exam with clear usted commands and explain ECGs, echoes, stress tests, heart monitors and blood draws before you do them.

grammar.p: Start from the *yo* form of the present, drop the *-o*, and switch the vowel: *-ar* verbs take *-e*, *-er/-ir* verbs take *-a*. *respirar* → *respire*, *toser* → *tosa*, *abrir* → *abra*. Irregular *yo* forms carry over: *poner* (pongo) → *ponga*, *decir* (digo) → *diga*, *hacer* (hago) → *haga*. Stem changes carry over too: *apretar* (aprieto) → *apriete*.
ex: Respire hondo.
Take a deep breath.
Tosa fuerte, por favor.
Cough hard, please.
Abra la boca.
Open your mouth.
Apriete mi mano.
Squeeze my hand.

grammar.h: Reflexive commands: attach *se* and add the accent
grammar.p: Many exam verbs are reflexive (*sentarse, acostarse, quitarse, ponerse, relajarse*). In an affirmative command the pronoun is glued to the end: *siéntese*. The stress stays on the same syllable, but that syllable is now third from the end, so it needs a written accent: *acuéstese, quítese, póngase, relájese, vuélvase, súbase, quédese*. With two pronouns the same rule applies: *póngasela* (put it on), *quítesela* (take it off).
ex: Siéntese en la camilla, por favor.
Please sit on the exam table.
Quítese la camisa y póngase la bata.
Take off your shirt and put on the gown.
Acuéstese boca arriba.
Lie down on your back.
¿La bata? Póngasela, por favor.
The gown? Put it on, please.

grammar.h: Negative commands: the pronoun goes in front
grammar.p: In a negative usted command the pronoun is NOT attached; it goes between *no* and the verb, and the accent disappears: *Muévase* → *No se mueva*. *Preocúpese* → *No se preocupe*.
ex: No se mueva, por favor.
Please don't move.
No se preocupe, no duele.
Don't worry, it doesn't hurt.
No hable mientras le tomo la presión.
Don't talk while I take your blood pressure.

grammar.h: Preparing the patient: le voy a… / va a sentir…
grammar.p: Say what you're about to do with *ir a* + infinitive. The pronoun *le* (to you / on you) goes either before *voy* or attached to the infinitive — same meaning: *Le voy a tomar la presión* = *Voy a tomarle la presión*. Never use it twice. Warn about sensations with *Va a sentir…*. Ask for warnings with *Avíseme si…* + present tense.
ex: Le voy a escuchar el corazón.
I'm going to listen to your heart.
Voy a ponerle unos parches en el pecho.
I'm going to put some stickers on your chest.
Va a sentir un piquete.
You're going to feel a little prick.
Avíseme si siente dolor.
Let me know if you feel pain.

grammar.h: Tests: done, being done, going to be done
grammar.p: Use the preterite for a test that is finished (*Le hicimos un electrocardiograma ayer*), *estar* + gerund for what is happening now (*Le estoy escuchando el corazón*), *ir a* for what's next (*Le vamos a hacer un ecocardiograma*), and the present perfect with *ya / alguna vez* (*¿Alguna vez le han hecho una prueba de esfuerzo?*).
ex: La semana pasada le hicimos un ecocardiograma.
Last week we did an echocardiogram on you.
Un momento, le estoy escuchando los pulmones.
One moment, I'm listening to your lungs.
Mañana le vamos a poner un monitor.
Tomorrow we're going to put a monitor on you.
¿Ya le han sacado sangre hoy?
Have they drawn your blood yet today?

phrases: Siéntese en la camilla, por favor.
Please sit on the exam table.
Quítese la camisa y póngase la bata, por favor.
Please take off your shirt and put on the gown.
Respire hondo… y aguante la respiración.
Take a deep breath… and hold it.
Le voy a tomar la presión.
I'm going to take your blood pressure.
Le voy a escuchar el corazón y los pulmones.
I'm going to listen to your heart and lungs.
You're going to feel a little prick.
Va a sentir el gel un poco frío.
The gel is going to feel a little cold.
Avíseme si siente dolor o mareo.
Let me know if you feel pain or dizziness.
We're done. You can get dressed.

items.q: How do you tell a patient "Please sit down"?
items.why: sentarse → (yo) me siento → usted command siente + se → siéntese. Siéntate is the tú form; siéntase comes from sentirse ("feel").

items.q: Por favor, ___ boca arriba en la camilla.
items.qen: Please lie down on your back on the exam table.
items.why: acostarse → (yo) me acuesto → acueste + se → acuéstese. Acuéstate is tú, which you don't use with patients.

items.q: Respire ___ por la boca.
items.qen: Take a deep breath through your mouth.
items.why: "Respire hondo" is the set phrase for a deep breath.

items.q: Ahora aguante la ___.
items.qen: Now hold your breath.
items.why: After the article la you need the noun: la respiración.

items.q: For the echo, you want the patient lying on his left side. What do you say?
items.why: Acuéstese = lie down; del lado izquierdo = on the left side. The others say right side, sit, or stand up.

items.q: ___ voy a escuchar el corazón.
items.qen: I'm going to listen to your heart.
items.why: With body parts Spanish uses the indirect object for the person: le (to you) + el corazón. Lo/la would make the person the direct object, which doesn't work with "el corazón".

items.q: Voy a ___ unos parches en el pecho.
items.qen: I'm going to put some stickers on your chest.
items.why: Infinitive after voy a, with le (on you) attached: ponerle. Lo/la don't fit because the thing being put is unos parches.

items.q: Va a ___ el gel un poco frío.
items.qen: The gel is going to feel a little cold (to you).
items.why: Sentir = to feel; sentar = to seat. After va a you need the infinitive.

items.q: No ___, por favor. Estoy haciendo el electrocardiograma.
items.qen: Please don't move. I'm doing the ECG.
items.why: Negative usted command: the pronoun goes in front and is not attached → no se mueva.

items.q: In a stress test, what is "la caminadora"?
items.why: La caminadora is the treadmill the patient walks on.

items.q: How do you say "a blood test"?
items.why: Un análisis de sangre = blood test. Prueba de esfuerzo = stress test; radiografía = X-ray.

items.q: Before an echo the patient asks, "¿Me va a doler?" Best reply?
opts: Sí, le va a doler mucho.
No, no duele. Va a sentir el gel y un poco de presión.
items.why: An echo is painless; the probe presses a little. "No me duele" talks about you, and "no le dolió" is past.

items.q: Quítese la camisa y ___ la bata.
items.qen: Take off your shirt and put on the gown.
items.why: ponerse → (yo) me pongo → ponga + se → póngase, accent on the first syllable.

items.q: You're examining a 75-year-old patient. Which is correct?
items.why: relajarse is an -ar verb → relaje + se → relájese. Relájate is tú; relájase has the wrong vowel; se relajó is past tense, not a command.

items.q: Si siente palpitaciones, ___ la hora en el diario.
items.qen: If you feel palpitations, write down the time in the diary.
items.why: Instruction to a patient → usted command: apunte.

items.q: Ask: "Have you ever had an echocardiogram?"
opts: ¿Alguna vez le han hecho un ecocardiograma?
¿Alguna vez le van a hacer un ecocardiograma?
¿Alguna vez le han hacido un ecocardiograma?
items.why: "Ever" → present perfect with the irregular participle hecho: le han hecho (have they done on you). Hacido does not exist.

items.q: What does "Le voy a sacar sangre" mean?
opts: I'm going to check your blood pressure.
I'm going to give you a shot.
I'm going to draw your blood.
items.why: Sacar sangre = to draw blood; voy a = I'm going to.

items.q: Va a sentir un ___.
items.qen: You're going to feel a little prick.
items.why: Un piquete is the everyday word (especially in Mexico) for a needle stick or prick.

items.q: Durante la prueba, avíseme si ___ dolor de pecho o mareo.
items.qen: During the test, let me know if you feel chest pain or dizziness.
items.why: Si (if) + present tense for a real possibility. Neither the present subjunctive nor the future is used right after si.

items.q: ¿La bata? ___, por favor.
items.qen: The gown? Put it on, please.
items.why: Affirmative usted command with two pronouns attached in one word: póngase + la → póngasela. Póntela is tú; pronouns can't go in front in an affirmative command; pongásela has the accent on the wrong syllable.

items.q: Por favor, ___ en la camilla.
items.en: Please sit on the exam table.
items.why: sentarse → siente + se → siéntese (accent because the stress is now third from last).

items.q: Ahora ___ hondo.
items.en: Now take a deep breath.
items.why: -ar verb → -e: respire.

items.q: Ahora ___ la respiración.
items.en: Now hold your breath.
items.why: -ar verb → -e: aguante.

items.q: Por favor, ___ la camisa.
items.en: Please take off your shirt.
items.why: quitarse → quite + se → quítese.

items.q: Por favor, ___ la camisa.
items.en: Please unbutton your shirt.
items.why: desabrocharse → desabroche + se → desabróchese, accent on the stressed -bró-.

items.q: Por favor, ___ la bata.
items.en: Please put on the gown.
items.why: ponerse → (yo) pongo → ponga + se → póngase.

items.q: Ahora ___ del lado izquierdo.
items.en: Now lie down on your left side.
items.why: acostarse (o→ue) → acueste + se → acuéstese.

items.q: Por favor, no ___.
items.en: Please don't move.
items.why: Negative command: pronoun in front → no se mueva.

items.q: Voy a ___ la presión.
items.en: I'm going to take your blood pressure.
items.hint: tomar, with the pronoun for "you" attached
items.why: The pronoun can attach to the infinitive: voy a tomarle (= le voy a tomar).

items.q: Le voy a ___ sangre del brazo.
items.en: I'm going to draw blood from your arm.
items.why: Sacar sangre = to draw blood (extraer is more formal; tomar sangre is also heard). After voy a, use the infinitive.

items.q: Por favor, ___ la boca.
items.en: Please open your mouth.
items.why: -ir verb → -a: abra.

items.q: Ahora ___ fuerte, por favor.
items.en: Now cough hard, please.
items.why: -er verb → -a: tosa.

items.q: Por favor, ___ quieto.
items.en: Please stay still.
items.why: quedarse → quede + se → quédese.

items.q: Un momento, le estoy ___ el corazón.
items.en: One moment, I'm listening to your heart.
items.why: estar + gerund for an action in progress: estoy escuchando.

items.q: Si siente palpitaciones, ___ el botón del monitor.
items.en: If you feel palpitations, press the button on the monitor.
items.why: apretar (e→ie): aprieto → apriete.

items.q: ¿Ya le ___ sangre hoy?
items.en: Have they already drawn your blood today?
items.why: Present perfect with ya: han sacado.

items.q: La semana pasada le ___ un ecocardiograma.
items.en: Last week we did an echocardiogram on you.
items.why: Finished event last week → preterite: hicimos.

items.q: El ecocardiograma nos muestra cómo ___ su corazón.
items.en: The echocardiogram shows us how your heart pumps.
items.why: General fact, present tense, subject su corazón → bombea.

items.q: ¿El parche? Ya ___ quité.
items.en: The patch? I already took it off you.
items.hint: two pronouns: to you + it (el parche)
items.why: le + lo becomes se lo: ya se lo quité.

items.q: Por favor, ___ la manga.
items.en: Please roll up your sleeve.
items.why: subirse → suba + se → súbase.

items.say: Acuéstese boca arriba, por favor.
opts: Lie down on your back, please.
Lie down on your stomach, please.
Lie on your left side, please.

items.say: Respire hondo y aguante la respiración.
opts: Take a deep breath and let it out.
Take a deep breath and hold it.

items.say: Le voy a poner unos parches en el pecho.
opts: I put some stickers on your chest.
I'm going to put some stickers on your chest.
I'm going to put some patches on your back.
You're going to put some stickers on your chest.

items.say: Va a sentir el gel un poco frío.
opts: The gel is going to feel warm.
You felt that the gel was cold.
I'm going to feel the gel a little cold.
The gel is going to feel a little cold to you.

items.say: Lleve el monitor puesto y apunte sus síntomas.
opts: Keep the monitor on and write down your symptoms.
Take off the monitor and write down your symptoms.
Bring the monitor back and tell us your symptoms.
Keep the monitor on and call us about your symptoms.

items.say: Ya le sacamos sangre esta mañana.
opts: We're going to draw your blood this morning.
We still haven't drawn your blood.
